review:
Now I've never played a Shadowrun game before, however I'm not exactly new to  turn based/strategy RPG games, having played games in a similar vein like the Shin Megami Tensei: Devil Survivor series and Fire Emblem. However, I'll be the first to admit I'm far from a veteran in the genre.

One of the key things I think Returns did right, is the tricky task of drawing me into the story immediately. It's pretty simple: your friend is dead, he's left you a "dead man's switch" - a recorded message promising a hefty reward if you can find the killer. OK. I'm in.

As for the ease of playing the game... as someone who's often daunted by complex RPG interfaces with endless choices, decisions, and items to equip, I thought Shadowrun's interface is a breeze. It clearly shows you your weapon slots, inventory slots, and which body parts you can equip on armor or modifications. As for playing the game itself, you can simply click on your HUD to switch between weapons or end turns, but there are hotkeys for the more practiced player, too.

You encounter many characters on your way to solve your friend's murder, and you get to pick and choose your own team of Shadowrunners to go on every mission with you. Each has their own specialty - summoning mechs, specializing in "decking" (hacking), melee combat, guns, magic, and so on, and I had a great time testing out all the different classes.

All of the characters have their own specialties, but the game is forgiving, and you could probably get by just using guns on everyone. I realized one of my runners had a healing ability 3/4 of the way through the game, and had been getting by just fine without knowing that. So if you're worried about difficulty or complexity, don't be.

Another positive for me is the game is heavily text based. There is a lot more discovery and reading than combat. You can also save anywhere except an NPC turn in combat, or in conversation. So I could get up to answer the door or grab some food without bothering to pause, or quit at a moment's notice if my friends asked me to play a multiplayer game.

I know I'm writing a review no one will ever read, for a two year old game, but it gets an easy recommendation from me, especially if you're a busy person who can only enjoy games in bits and pieces before you're on the go again.

It plays a lot like the new X-Com on a more personal scale, and a lot more choice when it comes to combat. Since it includes a lot of RPG elements and the Shadowrun setting, you can create a character any way you like, from a run-and-gunner to a mage slinging fireballs, to a mage slinging buffs, to a mage with a pet, or something in-between. 

Some things seem unpolished or foolish, however, like running a melee combatant or a physad; The few times I tried to melee an opponent, even with a physad NPC, I got chopped into hamburger. I'm also unsure why you'd want to stick with pistols when rifles and shotguns are available, no matter how good pistols get later in the game. Maxing out pistol skills seems silly. Similarly, some of the etiquette skills are nearly useless, while some are indispensable. I suppose that's true in life as well, but it's easy to feel annoyed that you've wasted your skill points.

But the setting is fantastic, and feels like it was written by people who know the game and want to make it as authentic and immersive as possible.

The archetypes such as Decker and Mage available at character creation simply assign the majority of your Karma for you. If you want full control over creating your character, it's better not to pick one.

Etiquettes aren't particularly useful in the Dead Man's Switch base campaign, but Academic will net you a decent chunk of cash early on while Shadowrunner and Corporate will come up the most often.

Don't ignore skill bonuses given by outfits. For example a Rigger will gain access to the incredibly powerful +2 AP bonus for drones at Drone Combat 9 which can be reduced to 8 by wearing an outfit increasing the skill by 1. Due to the way the skill system works, this single point is worth a whopping 27 Karma.

Conjured spirits have a chance to go berserk at the end of each turn, so it's best to keep them away from your party and close to the enemy to make sure the spirit goes after them first should you get unlucky.

Action Points are the most valuable resource in combat, so boosting your AP with things like the Haste spell while reducing the enemies' AP with things like concussion grenades can give a large edge in combat.

Ranged Combat 3 (or Melee Combat 3) opens up your third weapon slot. This is especially useful for Rigger/Deckers who need three slots for a cyberdeck and two drones.

While specialization is generally recommended, lightly dipping into other skills is cheap and often effective. A Shaman can expand their options by getting some Mage spells for example.

Cyberware hugely hinders a character's magical abilities. A physical class equipped with cyberware can consider some light investment in magic in order to gain access to simple buffs or magical healing, but on the opposite end pure spellcasters should avoid cyberware entirely.

Unlike all other weapons in the game, sniper rifles get less accurate the closer you are to the enemy.
The highest-end guns in the game all utilize a Smartlink. When choosing cyberware, make sure you have a datajack if you want to take advantage of this.

Good Indie game, cyberpunk theme. Very cool

I hesitated in picking up this game after reading a lot about how terrible the original campaign was and how the game was dull and boring. It also didn't help that I didn't really know anything about the Shadowrun universe. During the Summer Sale though, I was in the mood for something new, and picked it up. I just finished playing through the original campaign (Dead Man's Switch - DMS) and have to say, I'm glad I bought the game.

Getting the basics out of the way, I admit that DMS is very linear. There is a lot of reading involved. And besides combat, there's not a lot of interaction with the world. Still, as someone who knew next to nothing about Shadowrun before I started, I think DMS does a very good job of introducing the player to the world and the mythos surrounding it. The reading will probably be boring to someone who is deeply familiar with the setting, but I found it very useful. Gameplay is likewise straightforward which allows a new player to dive in without fear of messing up. I played a Street Samurai / Decker and had no trouble. I did find myself wishing I could build a party and level them up, outfitting them and whatnot ala Baldur's Gate, but perhaps that will happen in an expansion.

All in all, this game was well worth the $4 I paid. I also picked up the DLC, which I read is much better - I look forward to trying that next.

Gritty neon-rain-covered cyberpunk at it's finest. This game is a gem! 

When you start looking into your best friends death a deadly string of events are unfolded. You meet a lot of people along the way, but who can you really trust? The choices you make have an impact on the story and the combat system is rather balanced even if I keep forgetting I could use magic when I got mages with me.

The game is not centuries long and does not take forever to play through, but the replay value makes it good enough for both a second and a third run. A shadowrun.

Elves, trolls and cyberhardware mixed with ancient magic and a society where the rich are rich and the poor live in the slums with nothing.

Play it. You won't regret it.

The SNES Shadowrun was the jewel of my cartridge collection. I've honestly lost count of how many times I've played through it. With that in mind I started up my journey into Shadowrun Returns with a healthy dose of nostalgia and optimism, and at the end of the journey I came away happy, if not entirely satisfied.

Unlike the Shadowrun of yore, Returns plays like an odd crossing of point & click adventure and turn-based strategy. Your runner is investigating the death of an old friend, and in each scene spends most of their time navigating dense dialogues with the many NPCs on hand. You might also be tasked to click on an object or a door, but the vast majority of the non-combat gameplay is talking. It's good talking, though, with some very colorful characters and attentive writing. The parentheticals get a little too heady and poetic for my tastes, but they set the scenes well enough. Overall the game nails the Shadowrun setting, which goes a long way towards keeping me interested.

Combat is the other side of the coin, and while it works better than the ancient art of "stand in place and shoot forever", it's not without its flaws. Your crew and the enemy forces each take turns expending the action points of their members on a grid map with cover objects, much like in the recent XCOM. AP is spent a little oddly, however. Each move within a certain range costs one AP, whether it be a single step or a dash to the edge of their range. With melee weapons this is fine because the melee attack is included with the move, but ranged weapons cost at least one AP just to fire, so getting into an ideal position and firing can be a costly proposition. Doubly so when the sight lines around the environments are not terribly consistent, and it costs a full AP just to reload. It's an imperfect system that works well enough, but could definitely use more polish.

There are plenty of ways to kill people though, and enough skill points to earn through the game to make the most of them. You have melee, five different firearm types, drones, and two kinds of magic, and that's not even getting into the support skills. Unfortunately, there's not much reason to diversify, and the game even tells you as much. High ranks in skills are very powerful, and spreading your points around won't give you the ranks you need to pass skill checks or hit later enemies. Plus, you hire party members from a large roster of shadowrunners who can easily fill in the gaps for you.

These gripes are really part of a larger trend with Returns. You can buy weapons, armor, and other upgrades, but they are unevenly spaced throughout the game. There's not much to interact with in the many levels, and no real branching paths to explore. You can be a decker and get into the Matrix side battles, but they are few and far between. Your hired runners have no personality and can't be interacted with other than ordered around in battle. Even the story, built on some genuinely good writing, is small in scope and lacks any sort of proper build-up. It all points to a game not fully realized, a lot of potential without a lot of substance. The whole time I was playing, Returns felt more like a demo for the game engine than a full product.

That's not to say it wasn't fun. I thoroughly enjoyed the 8-10 hours it took to complete, and aside from a particularly annoying final mission, had no major complaints about it. The issue is more a lot of little shortcomings mounting to give Returns a very half-baked feel. It's definitely worth playing, and I'm very interested to follow it with Dragonfall, but I wouldn't fault anyone who checked out after a few hours. Shadowrun Returns is a good enough Shadowrun game, and now I want a better one.

Hype and expectation are funny things. They can invite even the most rational and level-headed into wish fulfulment FAR beyond the truth, and we all know how prevalent that is in video gaming. I honestly believe that this game's reputation absolutely suffers from precisely this, especially from the view of some players. 

So, Shadowrun Returns - the question is "does it", or rather "does it REALLY warrant the return?" 

Let's start with the expectation part I mentioned. When this game was proposed, those that were fans of the old tabletop RPG and the old SNES classic sat up and took notice, and for good reason. Nostalgia aside, both are truly excellent games in their own rights. The downside to this is that it tends to set the bar VERY high, expectation-wise.

Fast forward to the game's release, and there were certainly mixed views; much of the criticism dealt with there being less on the action and more on the text and story. Also, length was cited too, or rather, lack of it. On the face of it, very valid criticisms, except that many of these either forgot or didn't understand WHAT the game was achieving - a new version of the classic games, adhering closely to the rules - in short, Shadowrun RETURNS. The clue's in the name. It does what it says on the tin.

So, there's an abundance of text and story, and less of the action itself, and yes, it is a bit short. While they are valid concerns EVERY game buyer should consider before dropping their cash, context is also equally important. Apologies for this slightly overblown introduction, but I felt it valid to lay this down at the outset. Let's get on with the review.

If you know what Shadowrun is (or was), then there's little point in going over this and you can skim to the last paragraph. If you don't, then as I've already said, there's the classic tabletop "D&D style" game - a pure, unadulterated old-school pencil and paper RPG. The hook here is that elves, orcs, goblins and all the staples of fantasy exist, but the one major difference is everything is a futuristic sci-fi bent. It probably sounds completely at odds with one another, but it works so very, very well, both in lore and in combat ... ESPECIALLY in combat. You can still hack 'n' slash if you want to, you can still use magic if you want to, but add to the mix firearms and a complete veneer of futuristic and modern tech, and you have Shadowrun.

It rather goes without saying that anyone who has spent any time playing old-school tabletop RPG knows that story and text are perhaps the premier parts, and that is the case here, naturally. But the question to the critics remains "ah, but it is any good?" Thankfully, the answer is "yes, it is".

I confess I'm a little jaded. I've been around gaming since the very start, and have never had a period when I've not been involved. I've seen a lot, played a lot, own a lot, and have even worked in the industry (albeit relatively briefly). For the most part, I care little for story in games - most times I'm merely concerned with the mechanics over everything else. I couldn't tell you the story of Halo, for example, as it never gripped me in any way. So, why on earth am I saying this game's story is good? Because it DID grip me right from the off. It works. You know the story's working on you when you can start to identify and remember the characters. So, being heavy on the story is an ASSET to this game, and in no way a hindrance. I shan't spoil it in any way, but it's a fairly standard story, but it does it pretty well, so in summary I don't see the critique of "too much story, too little action" in any way a bad thing unless it's REALLY not your thing.

Now, onto length. Yes, it IS relatively short. However, you should at least consider the reasoning behind the game's existence - it would never have seen the light of day AT ALL were it not for crowd-funding. Sure, you can claim they made big promises and ran out of resources and/or time, but the conclusion here is that putting all those aside the end product is pretty damned good. As stated before, it very much does what it says on the tin. So, if you don't mind quantity being less if the quality's good or reasonable, then there is no issue here. What does render the length argument completely invalid is one thing - WORKSHOP support. There's TONS of user-generated content out there which not only mimics what tabletop RPGs are all about, but the inclusion of mod tools (which I haven't tried) ensure that it's pretty easy to dole out a good scenario, and it certainly shows. So, if you finish the game and want more, you won't be disappointed at all.

The combat is best described as being very similar to XCOM. It's turn-based with the dual-turn set of movement/action phases per character, or a mixture of those: you move, you shoot/swing/etc, and your turn's over. Your playfield is peppered with objects that you can utilize as cover, with the shield icon offering how good that cover is. This all offers a lovely tactical play where you don't just consider dumping your character up against the enemy and swing away at them, but you have to consider balancing cover with line of sight, flanking, and a number of other little tricks to make the best use of the battle.

Character skills are great. As you'd rightly expect from a combination fantasy/sci-fi, it lends you a VERY wide palette of things to mess around with. Fire-based magic attacks? Sure. Rifles, pistols, or SMGs? Yup, have at them. Fire-based attacks WITH your pistol? Yup, that too. It does the Shadowrun rules well, and the interface is clear and intuitive and you'll have no issues picking it up quickly.

Visually, the game offers a very nice art-style that does the medium justice. Backgrounds are all pre-rendered and hand-drawn (or at least they LOOK hand-drawn) in a graphic novel style which suits perfectly. Nothing I can fault here at all. Musically, the soundstrack is really good. I'm not a big fan of music soundtracks - I'm not one who will listen to them outside of the game. To me, they're a background that serves to provide ingredient to the recipe. They should illustrate without hindering the game in any way. Not only does the style and mood of the music suit perfectly, but it's not repetitive, and remains interesting without hindering in ANY way. If you're someone who does listen to game music absent of the game, you might well find this one very appealing.

So, final summary time. Is it worth purchasing? Yes. If you are expecting a good turn-based old-shool RPG, it's worth it. Steam Workshop really underlines this, value-wise. The only caveat I would make is that if you're either not sure whether this sort of game's for you, or the length of the official game really is an issue for you, I'd thoroughly recommend waiting for a sale - it's still worth picking up.

Final note I'm doing with all my reviews now: I'm giving a "what do I think the game's worth?" instead of any score or other metric, as I think that's the most valuable metric anyone could have. I'd say this deserves a £9 (or your regional equivalent).

[h1] Shadowrun Returns is a lone-wolf style, turn-based strategy with [i]RPG elements[/i], set in the year 2054 within the gritty underbelly of Seattle, combining an urban cyberpunk fantasy with the abrasive narrative of a seasoned crime novel.



Be prepared for a lot of reading.[/h1]
The steam showcase videos appear to stress heavily on combat but this is misleading, as there is a lot of text to be read, and no voice acting; very disappointing after hearing the trailer. 

Despite being excellently written, with interesting location descriptions (if a little verbose,) and crafty dialogue, the campaign was short and uninspired - your standard murder mystery with a sci-fi twist. ONCE AGAIN, so, so many grammatical errors! In a text-heavy game, this is unacceptable, whether developed under a small budget or one of millions, I can not fully appreciate nor take a game seriously when such simple errors are so obviously overlooked.
Note that Shadowrun Returns is 100% linear, which I believe is the biggest flaw, with few slim chances to deviate from the main storyline, and very few side quests - certainly not what I consider to be a 'proper' RPG. Only toward end game did the stagnant plot become mildly interesting, and the combat more frequent, which is a shame as enemy encounters are really fun!


Combat offers turn-based tactical play with plenty of scattered objects to hide behind and utilise as cover - similar to the XCOM format. AI is intelligent, so making the best use of your surroundings is important and the consideration of placement and enemy flanking should be taken into account.


Character skills are first-rate, and the UI is intuitive. Never falling short of different tactical styles, you can combine the best of both to singe and slaughter, or take the direct approach and pepper your foes with bullets. A 'jack of all trades, master of none' approach will do you no favours here though, and the game appears to encourage specialisation in only a few fields. This may initially seem unappealing, but you will constantly hire temporary runners from all walks of life and skillset. This [i]does[/i] dismantle the feeling of a team structure, though allows easy access for playing around with other builds to your tactical advantage - if you have the dough to pay for their services. 
(Runner work doesn't come cheap ya know!)


Wonderful art and design style with beautifully detailed character portraits and a 2D, seemingly hand-painted backdrop does this game justice, but is marred by awful, janky character models, which leave a lot to be desired. The soundtracks perfectly compliment the art style, capturing the industrialised futuristic theme, and psyching you to get down and dirty. 


Replayability is pretty much nonexistent in the main campaign unless you wish to test yourself with varying degrees of difficulty. I personally am in no way compelled to revisit this particular story again, and yes, it is relatively short. However, with workshop support, there is DREK-LOADS of user-generated content available, expanding the universe and adhering to the D&D theme of its successor.



As a Kickstarter crowdfunded game and a remake of the original tabletop Shadowrun Role-Playing game, I can understand the hype but can't say that this is anything special. 

I did have a small measure of fun, but perhaps my high expectations of the game had a negative impact on my experience, perhaps even, the clue in the title (Returns) alluded to potential differences from its predecessor. 
Still, it scraped the bar in terms of enjoyment for me but is ultimately interesting enough to entice me toward the other titles in the series. 'Only just' a positive review, definitely worth a play for previous Shadowrun title fans if bought on sale, but don't expect a triple-A game.

Finally finished Shadowrun Returns. I played it when it first released way back in 2013, but only played about 1/2 of the game. I got distracted by other shiny games or something . . . squirrel!

Anyway, just finished it tonight. Great story, superb writing, but the story got a little out there at the end. But, that's ok. It was enjoyable from start to finish. 

The combat is very well done, yet fairly simple, turn-based combat XCOM style that we're all familiar with. There were still plenty of opportunites for interesting tactics to keep the battles fun and compelling.

This is the first game in the Shadowrun trilogy, Dragonfall and Hong Kong being the sequels. You can tell the developers were still figuring stuff out and had not perfected their wonderful game engine and story quite yet. 

I look forward to starting Dragonfall: Director's Cut next. This is the one that everyone raves about as being the best in class. I'm getting started right away.

Anyway, Shadowrun Returns was a great way to spend 28-30 hours (I have a total of 40+ from playing earlier and starting over). 

Highly recommended for you turn-based combat with light to medium RPG aspects, and a good story with LOTS of reading. You gotta read to enjoy this one. Which is a good thing! 

Have fun with whatever game you choose to play, fellow gamer friends! Huzzah!  :cupup:

If you're expecting an RPG with open world and long hours of playing, this is not for you.

This is a short (I finished it in about 12 hours of gameplay, not rushing or anything) and linear (at no point there is even an option of doing something different, picking different ways, or other stuff you would expect from an RPG) game.

That being said, during those 12 hours I had a nice time. The story is interesting, the gameplay & interface is enjoyable, and for a simple game with no voice acting, the atmosphere is amazing.

I would definitely recommend if you find this at a discount. Well worth if a few bucks for the 12 hour fun - just don't expect it to be a super production.

Warning: I might be biased.
I have been a player of the Shadowrun tabletop RPG for almost 30 years and this game captures the atmosphere of that game perfectly. No wonder, since people who created the RPG in the first place were involved in the development of this computer game. The text descriptions and dialogues are very well done. To me as a hardcore Shadowrun fan this game is absolutely perfect and everything i ever wanted from a SR compuer game.
i have no idea how people without knowledge of the Shadowrun lore are experiencing this game. There are no voice-over dialogues, flashy cutscenes, impressive 3D graphics or 7,1 Dobly Atmos surround sound. But if you don't mind reading a lot of text and you liked games liked Baldurs Gate or Planescape Torment, because of the way the story was presented in those games, then Shaodwrun Returns might be worth a look for you, even if you don't know (yet) what Renraku, UCAS or Halloweeners are. Shadowrun's greatest asset always was its rich lore and world and you can find it here in droves.

This game is worth playing if : 
- you're a fan of the Shadowrun universe
- you somehow liked the Snes Shadowrun game (even though they're really different gameplay-wise)
- you want to learn the basis about the Shadowrun Returns games before playing Dragonfall and Hong Kong
- you want to meet Harlequin (seriously, that man is funny). 

This is the order in which I suggest you to play the Shadowrun Returns games in order to fully enjoy the experience : 

Shadowrun Returns > Shadowrun: Dragonfall > Shadowrun: Hong Kong > Shadowrun Returns

Replaying Shadowrun Returns last will allow you to really enjoy it, since going through the 2 others will allow you to better know the game's story and gameplay.

Shadowrun Returns is an great isometric turn-based RPG with a vast amount of lore behind it. Lovely! 
 
[b]❤️️ Pros ❤️️[/b]
[list]
[*]The game is based on the already established Shadowrun universe. Because of that, there is a lot of lore in place already allowing for great depth and detail in the world that you play in. 
[*]The story is good, albeit a little bit predictable. Even though you know what is coming, it is interesting enough to see how everything unfolds. 
[*]Graphics are okay - together with the music they really set the tone to create a cyberpunk-like ambience, but no amazing graphics card needed here. 
[*]Gameplay is alright - don't expect huge depth here, but it feels like an "XCOM Lite". There's cover and RNG when it comes to hitting your target, but it doesn't go much deeper than that. Enemy AI isn't that smart, generally they run up to you and attack.  
[*]There are uniquely named classes, such as the "Street Samurai" and the "Decker" which brings a little diversity to the standard Warrior/Mage/Thief standards.
[/list]

[b]❌ Cons ❌[/b]
[list]
[*]There is no spoken dialogue. For a game that's very dialogue-heavy (basically, outside of combat you are talking) this felt like a missed opportunity. The game was funded through a (very successful) kickstarter campaign and that might have made it harder to find good voice actors, but that doesn't make it less boring. 
[*]The game is linear. There are optional quests but they are nothing more than a single-map side quest, to then continue down the line that the main quest has laid out for you. Nothing you choose at the start of the game (race/gender/class) affects what you'll end up seeing, besides some dialogue changes. There is an illusion of choice, but no matter how good or evil you are, you always end up going down the same path. 
[*]It's not a very long game. I heard that the other games in the trilogy were longer, but don't expect this game to take more than 20 hours.

[/list]

[b]Final thoughts[/b]
Shadowrun Returns is a good (re)introduction to the Shadowrun universe. While it's not an outstanding game, I'd recommend playing it for the cool lore. Definitely consider getting it on a sale.

[h1]IN A WORD: [b]WORTHWHILE[/b] [/h1] 
[h1]IN SHORT:[/h1]
[quote=]
[b]SIMILAR GAMEPLAY TO:[/b] Jagged Alliance 2, Jagged Alliance: Flashback, Wasteland 2
[b]WHAT TO EXPECT:[/b] Basic kick-starter funded game. Short story.  Very limited RPG.  Cyberpunk themed.  Single-player. Virtually linear.  Great tactical combat.  Great graphics and art direction.  Superb writing.

[b]STATUS:[/b] COMPLETE.
[b]WHEN TO BUY:[/b]  ASAP for fans.  Otherwise a good sale.[/quote]

[i]More info below....[/i]

[h1]THE LOWDOWN:[/h1]
Shadowrun Returns is a story-driven, party-oriented RPG with tactical combat.  The action takes place a in dysoptic cyberpunk version of Seattle around the year 2050 where trolls, elves and dwarves live alongside humanity.  The heavy use of stimulants and cybernetics pervade most aspects of life.  Magic exists.  Crime, and drug-taking are rife.  The internet has become an alternate reality where anything goes.  Rich and powerful corporations hold sway over everything and everyone, resulting in prevalence of industrial espionage carried out by Shadowrunners. These are mercenaries for hire who will perform any job if the price is right.  

Players take on the role of a shadowrunner character and specialize in many abilities becoming a warrior, hacker, drone operator, magic user and unarmed combat specialist or a mix thereof.  The game world is shown in isometric form across a dozen or so fixed locations.  Play alternates between real-time exploration and investigation during the adventure phase and turn-based tactical combat.  Additional party members can be hired from an extensive roster of NPCs before going into battles, on a temporary basis.  The game begins with the player investigating who committed the murder and why, but this will ultimately lead to much greater quest with much direr consequences.  Are you up to the assignment?

[h1]THE GOOD:[/h1]
+ A very good story with fantastic writing.  Even if some gamers may find it too much!
+ Strong combat dynamic across a variety of categories: Magic, drones, ranged combat, melee and unarmed.
+ Superb range of tactical combat options; from specialized firing modes, overwatch, to reloading without using an action.  Most become available by leveling certain stats.
+ Amazing array of character selection and customization.
+ Wonderfully created cyberspace levels reminiscent of System Shock, that plays like the tactical combat.
+ A large array of equipment and items, with better items only becoming available as the story progresses.
+ Very well balanced if a too easy for hardcore RPGers.
+ Lots of well-made custom scenarios available in Steam Workshop.
+ Ace production from its crisp, isometric graphics, well-drawn artwork and midi-based soundtrack (non-dlc), altogether produces a great ambience.
+ Strong easy to use and understand interface.

[h1]THE BAD:[/h1]
- Not open world.  Series of linked map areas.
- Too short with very linear gameplay.
- No voice-acting. Really could have done with it.
- Only a very few optional quests.  Needed a few more at least.

[h1]AND THE ORDINARY:[/h1]
* Needed more environment interaction with containers and searchable dead bodies to give the proper feel of an RPG.
* A few more vendors would have been nice.  But theres just enough to sell old or buy new items.

[h1]VERDICT:[/h1]
Shadowrun Returns is a really polished game.  For what it is, its a solid buy.  Built on a tight kickstarter budget it was designed to re-boot the franchise back to the video game format.  It has a very strong story with a neat twist.  Some great writing, complex RPG character building and  turn-based tactical combat with many possible choices.  One of the best features of the game is how it uses the isometric engine to make the sequences in cyberspace as relevant as the tactical combat.

However the lack of an (even semi) open-world and voice-overs resulted in an incomplete experience for me personally.  Maybe I wanted too much from this first outting; more of an open-world where places could be visited, more NPCs to talk to in the background.  Just more padding, to add to the overall atmosphere.  Perhaps even more of a permanent party with more control over their stats.  But that doesnt take away from this first decent effort.

Others have said that this feels more like you are taking part in an interactive video novel, a linear story where you are more of a passenger than the driver, like you should tend to feel when playing RPGs.  I agree with this but even for a casual Shadowrun fan like me, its enough to ensure that the franchise is back on PC.  For that I am thankful.

All-in-all Shadowrun Returns feels like an entry level adventure.  Thats not a bad thing afterall because it is the first of the latest series, of modern adaptations to PC.  In this the developers have done a great job to make the game accessible, enjoyable, mostly accurate to the pen & paper RPG but most of all, to leave the player wanting more.  Shadowrun Returns sticks to the addage walk before you run and if this is built upon in the follow-on games (Dragonfall and Hongkong), then I wont complain.  

As it is I would only recommend playing this if you are after an easy albeit interesting introduction to the world of Shadowrun or if you are a hardcore fan and want to play the current series from this developer, from the beginning.  I would suggest either way that you get this on sale or in a bundle as Ive read that the other titles are superior.  Cant wait to try those out!

Shadowrun Returns is a turn-based cyberpunk themed strategy R.P.G. developed by Harebrained Schemes and published by Harebrained Holdings. Shadowrun has gained a huge cult following since its creation nearly 25 years ago. Now, creator Jordan Weisman returns to the world of Shadowrun, modernizing this classic game setting as a single player, turn-based tactical roleplaying game. The year is 2054 and magic has returned to the world awakening powerful creatures of myth and legend as technology merges with flesh and consciousness. As a shadowrunner, you're a mercenary living on the fringes of society, in the shadows of massive corporate arcologies, surviving day-by-day on skill and instinct alone. Shadowrun Returns harkens back to the classic old school roleplaying games from back in the day. The top-down isometic view, intense turn-based combat and non-voiced dialogue of a traditional R.P.G. are expertly blended in this fantastic indie title from Harebrained Holdings. The story is divided into campaigns which can range from solving murders to battling corporate espionage and a number of other different situations and once you've finished the games main storyline you can download new user created campaigns from the Steam Workshop or the Nexus which further extends the replayability of this great title.

Besides the excellent story, the turn-based combat of course is one of the best features of this game. Progressing through the narrative will reward you with experience points and allow you to grow your character in any direction that you choose. Want to summon spirits as an elven shaman, be an expert hacker or go guns and blade ablazing as a Street Samurai? The choice is up to you. As the leader of the group, it's also up to you to choose the right balance of combat, tech and magical abilities in order to have a successful run. The gripping tactical combat system is quick and responsive and just a fun alternative to the combat of today's more popular roleplaying games.

Graphically the game looks terrific in full high definition with its futuristic cyberpunk setting. The environments are also quite varied as you will travel from the slums of the Redmond Barrens to the extravagant offices of powerful corporations and beyond. The character portraits presented during conversations have a unique style that lends itself well to this title and I find the isometric backgrounds and set pieces delightful to view. One of my favorite things about these types of games are the small details in the world around you and this title is chock full of them and add to that some excellent sound effects and a terrific musical score and Shadowrun Returns delivers big time. 

If you're a R.P.G. fan looking for something a little different to add to your library or just enjoy old-school or retro games then I HIGHLY RECOMMEND Shadowrun Returns! You will not be dissapointed with this title.

Shadowrun Returns can easily be understood if you think of it as the love child between Blade Runner and Dungeons & Dragons.

The game drips attitude and personality, so much so the song It Can't Rain All the Time from the movie The Crow can feel perfectly at home here. You are a Shadowrunner, an individual who runs jobs outside of the black and white lines of the law for anyone willing to pay. The story greatly revolves around a Deadmans Switch which can be thought of as a last will and testimony sent to - in this case - an individual automatically when they die.

When your old Shadowrunner buddy Sam dies, you receive his Deadmans Switch asking for his killer to be caught for a handsome reward.

[h1]DIFFICULTY[/h1]

Level two costs 2 Karma points etc. The rest of the categories have some sub categories such as Spellcasting is under Willpower. Review update: Dragonfall

Dragonfall takes the formula established in the original release, and improves on it in several ways. Its actually misleading to describe this as "DLC". These days, particularly in the RPG genre, that term conjures up thoughts of short quests and meaningless item packs. Dragonfall is more like the good old days of expansion packs, where you got a meaty chunk of gameplay to sink your teeth into.

The story is excellent, one of the best I've played through in any game for quite some time. The action has shifted to Berlin, where you've joined a crew of shadowrunners on a contract to extract some data from a vault. Predictably, the mission goes wrong, dragging you into another deep conspiracy full of twists and turns, that also helps to explain more of the world's lore.

Because your crew are fully fleshed out characters, instead of the original's mostly hired help, each character has much more depth to their personality. They have a past, they have feelings, and the story is given increased emotional weight through conversations with these characters.

The gameplay mechanics, tactical turn based combat, and level up system all remain intact, and we now have the ability to save anywhere, rather than being limited to the original's checkpoint only system. Quest structure is less linear than before. You have some control over which order to play certain quests, and most quests have optional objectives that, if completed, provide greater (or alternate) rewards. You'll also have some tough moral choices to consider which affect quest outcomes, and many areas allow for the use of non combat skills, including talking your way past guards or hacking computers to gain information.

Dragonfall took me 19 hours to complete, which is significantly longer than the original game, and represents excellent value for money at full price. I don't recall encountering any bugs at all.

Overall Dragonfall is amazing, and I rate it as an absolute MUST BUY.

Shadowrun Returns is the first game in the rebooted Shadowrun trilogy, along with Dragonfall and Hong Kong. Being the first game, there's definitely some hitches in the game that hold it back from being as good as the ones later on down the line. For those new to the series, Shadowrun is a cyberpunk RPG series about being a "Shadowrunner" - expendable black ops people who undertake secret missions for the highest bidder, engaging in corporate warfare and the odd bit of world-saving.

The game plays like a streamlined X-COM: turn based tactical combat using cover and abilities and the occasional rage at RNG. A very streamlined version of the tabletop system is used, and all classic shadowrun archetypes are more or less supported through the vanilla campaign. Support in user generated content ("UGC") will vary by module. The artstyle is bright and colorful with stylized caricatures of people that let you immediately identify the different metahuman races in the game at a glance. Music is mostly ambient and honestly, mostly forgettable, but fits the feel and environments you're in.

The game setup is not that of an open world, but rather linear connected levels that you cannot return to once you're finished with them. Make sure you do all of your exploring before you move on, since there's no way to "farm" money or equipment or anything. I was a little disappointed because I originally thought it was a more open world game with more sidequests - the experience in all three games is very much a linear guided experience, so know that going in.

Archetypes and skill levelling all give you abilities you'll want to use constantly. Even something as simple as a 10% aim buff, or 2 armor, is worth spamming constantly. Offensive magic is powerful as well, but I had better luck spamming things like Haste, Armor, Aim, Heal, and Barriers for my team.

There are a few gripes with the game that I have that are for the most part solved in later games:
1: Summoning spirits is just bad, IMO. You can only do it in certain parts of certain maps, and you have to give up part of your shaman's turn to do so. The more actions you let the spirit take, the more likely it is to break free and turn hostile. Alternately you can spend money on a consumable to do it anywhere, but you still have to "feed" it action points a and it can still turn hostile. It felt like a very hamfisted approach to spirit summoning. Rigger drones were much more managable.
2: The AI has an incredible bias towards attacking the main character, and the MC's death is a game over. This pretty much forces you to make a very tanky character and max Body very quickly, unless you want to have to constantly hide your character. I didn't want to do that, so I went with a physical adept and stabbed everything to death with ranged backup.
3: Money can be pretty tight until the last third of the game. If you want to be a full roided out street samurai, you'll need to save money somewhere, and you may need to do that by hiring less runners. The game is soloable by street samurai and a correctly built physical adept, it's just difficult to do so. The game is also pretty good about giving you discounts on "important" NPCs, or mandatory hires (such as Deckers), so it's easy to save money while making an effective team on the cheap. Some of the NPC runners are definitely way better than the others. Make sure you get your money's worth.
4: I found Decking to be of limited use as a main character. It does let you access some hacking and side loot, but any mission critical situation, the game gives you a mandatory decker NPC you can use that can handle the situation just fine. The matrix sections aren't difficult, and add some fun parallel combat and exploration to realspace fights.

Overall the game is a pleasant experience, and feels like a Shadowrun game. There's not a lot of "choice" to be made. Dialog options mostly exist as a way for you to inject your character's flavor into the situation. Skill checks are sometimes called for in dialogs and let you access extra information, or have extra ways of approaching situations. Especially in the second half, the game's battle maps do very well at giving you a lot of different approaches to a situation based on your team composition. I would recommend the game to anyone looking for a medium length turn based tactical game, and anyone who enjoys the Cyberpunk aesthetic. The game often goes on sale for extremely cheap,  sub 5 dollars, so keep an eye out.

Until recently, I was somewhat reluctant to recommend this game. I enjoyed Dead Man's Switch, but, like many people, found it to be more of an interactive novel (with tactical interludes) than a role playing game. Playing around with the editor has been a blast, but I know that this isn't for everyone, and neither is playing through User Generated Content (though there's some excellent stuff out there). 

After the launch of Dragonfall, however, I can post the positive review with confidence. Aside from implementing the much needed save-anywhere system, Dragonfall is a much more engaging campaign on so many levels. It's what Dead Man's Switch should have been, but wasn't. While the main hub is relatively small, you really do feel like the leader of a team of Shadowrunners, and are able to take on a variety of jobs, and complete them in the order that you wish. The jobs themselves, more importantly, feel a great deal more open, with tough choices and multiple objectives, including optional points of interest. The literally two side quests you got in DMS felt like afterthoughts ("oh crap, we forgot to put side quests in and the game launches in a week!"). Here, everything feels lovingly attended to. This is, perhaps, a major advantage of text based story telling. If you're inclined to pick up the relatively robust editor that comes along with the base game, you'll not that your storytelling capacity is only limited by your writing ability and your imagination (the scripting and map building aren't that hard to learn). If you've got the desire and the ability to write, you can craft beautiful and interesting adventures, whether side quest or main, to your heart's content. And that's what HBS has done this time around.

In fact, the one thing that hasn't changed is the excellent writing. This isn't high end literature, but it's engaging and interesting all around. It draws you into the world and, in some cases, really captivates you. The charachters, especially your crew members, the fixer, and the occupants of your little slice of berlin, are memorable and interesting to a person. 

It's unfortunate that this had to be released as DLC. The base campaign had the writing down, but it didn't have the wow factor or the, well, interactivity. If only it had...The setting and the charachters of Dead Man's Switch could have really shone with a similar treatment.

Still, better late than never.

Shadowrun Returns is an old-school isometric cRPG in the vein of the classic Fallout games based on, as its title suggests, the Shadowrun franchise; one of the pioneers in the fictional literature best known for combining cyberpunk, magic, urban fantasy and crime elements into this unique lore. Initially started as a pen-and-paper boardgame, it was long “forgotten” by today’s generation or occasionally overshadowed by games such as the widely popular and highly-acclaimed Deus Ex – at least that is how I see it.

The gameplay in Shadowrun Returns is similar to many classic cRPGs. You manage a team of up to four Shadowrunners where you can choose from the story’s main characters to use or hire random, more specialised, Shadowrunners which suit your mission’s requirements. Just like in any RPG, you can pick a race and class for your character at the start, each with its own advantages and disadvantages. The combat mechanics are turn-based and generally well balanced, resembling the one used in the recently rebooted XCOM franchise by Firaxis Games, thus if you are familiar with it then that is good news because it is solid. In addition, by completing missions or triggering certain events in the story, karma points are earned to be further spent on enhancing your main character’s attributes which include the typical Strength, Intelligence and Charisma, to name a few, seen in most classic RPGs. For instance, investing lots of points into Intelligence allows your character to be highly competent with Decking or Drone Control specialities, or investing a lot into Charisma can unlock specific dialogue conversations to bypass certain key situations in the game (other attributes are used sometimes for exclusive dialogues too). In fact, the game does a good job in making sure the player cannot master all the available attributes, because as the game explains in its tips during loading screens: a jack of all trades is a master of none. As a whole, perhaps one of the key aspects of its gameplay aside from its good turn-based combat is how you can approach the narration by choosing your responses based on what personality you want your character to be like when talking to NPCs. While not all responses follow a choice-and-consequence pattern, some do actually have an impact on how things develope; and Shadowrun Returns provides a wide range of opportunities. Ultimately, this also increases the replayability of the game a great deal. One last addition is The Matrix which is like a cyberworld used by Deckers to hack into systems. It is an interesting concept but feels a bit underdeveloped as it can feel a bit of a chore most of times.

The art direction in Shadowrun Returns is at the very least appealing. The backgrounds, which do vary, are nicely drawn and the colour pallets used fit with Shadowrun’s universe and its cyberpunk roots, making it easily one of the best looking traditional isometric games out there.  The neon light effects used are also something to praise it for since they bring the game’s world to life, despite the lack of NPCs roaming the streets. Unfortunately, the character models, including their animations, are about the only things which look visually mediocre in this rather attractive game, almost making it look like it was ported from a mobile game. Moreover, Shadowrun Returns also boasts a brilliant soundtrack with a couple of memorable tracks, such as the one from the main menu (“Return of the Sixth World”) and “Puppet Masters”, which fit with the cyberpunk vibes of the game. Sure, while this soundtrack does sound slightly different to the one from the original Shadowrun game on SNES, it still sounds cool.

Without a shadow (no pun intended) of a doubt, Shadowrun Returns’ strongest aspect is its narration with its great character development. Whilst it takes a bit of time at the beginning to get to like (or despise) individuals you meet, eventually you will be surprised by how many who become your companions or allies will quickly turn out as memorable characters by the end with who you can at least sympathise. Starting off as a simple detective story in the style of Jack The Ripper which progressively deepens and deviates from just a simple detective case to solve later on, the “Dead Man’s Switch” story in Shadowrun Returns is mostly solid, even though it sorrowfully turns into a Fahrenheit (Indigo Prophecy) type of story in the last quarter of the journey. While it might not completely ruin the endgame experience, that latter part personally left me with a sour taste in my mouth. Despite featuring no voice acting, this does not ruin the experience either since it allows you to use your own imagination on how characters are supposed to sound like in the story. As a result, it might require a bit more effort and dedication to read some of its pompous written dialogues, and this will certainly not be everyone’s cup of tea.

Shadowrun Returns has some glarying imperfections though. Being an extremely linear (pretty much most of it is on rails) and story-driven game, it lacks any sense of exploration due to its contained maps and minimal interactions with their environments. This is something which might frankly turn off quite a number of RPG fans, old-school or contemporary. Clicking on certain hotspots, found only intermittently around places, usually pop up a text-box describing what the character is observing, but these are indeed very few throughout the game’s journey. For a text-heavy game, this aspect of interaction seems like a lost opportunity for further enriching the experience. On top of that, once a mission is completed or the area is cleared, in most cases there is no way to revisit an area afterwards. For a completionist, it is crucial to check everything prior to proceeding to the next area. The lack of a deep character customisation is another aspect that will not please every RPG fan out there since it is very basic and only allows you to choose from premade character models. Additionally, there is also no inventory customisation/management for your companions either which can cause some annoyances when planning your tactics prior or during combat.  One further frustration with the game’s design is its tendency to occasionally lock the player into combat even when everyone in the area is eliminated. This results in wasted time trying to move your team to the next objective location on the map as it is agonisingly slow due to its turn-based mechanics. And lastly, as much as the writing is top-notch, the game can sometimes drown you with its longwinded expositions from time to time which can be underwhelming especially for those looking to jump into action more often.

In conclusion, Shadowrun Returns is an adequate and faithful entry to the franchise, albeit a limited game, that should please any cRPG, cyberpunk/fantasy fans and even book readers out there to some degree. While it can honestly feel shallow in places, its stellar writing, good narration, memorable cast of characters, distinctive art direction and competent XCOM-like gameplay should keep most people invested in its relatively short 10+ hours campaign, even if its story loses some of its early charm near the end. This, however, remains a borderline recommendation as many things could have been done to further improve the game as a RPG since it can feel a bit basic. To get most out of it is to always remind yourself that it is a very story-driven experience foremost, so any notions of open-world or high-budget production values in the manner of The Elder Scrolls should be dismissed, otherwise you will be disappointed by your own misconceptions. The best way to describe Shadowrun Returns is like reading a long, but relatively good book (that will not really blow you away) accompanied by solid gameplay elements to justify it as a game -- because honestly, it is not too far from being no more than a visual novel.

DISCLAIMER: I usually review games after I've finished them (or at least the main quest). However, I believe I have a solid grasp on what makes this game special so I've decided to review it only six hours into the game. Some of my pros/cons may or may not extend throughout the entire game.

---

Shadowrun Returns is an exceptionally atmospheric cyberpunk RPG. Alluring neon colors are balanced by the dull grays of the concrete jungle. A murder mystery blossoms into a much more complex scenario that delves into the dark themes that are signature to this genre. The soundtrack evokes mystery and a sense of modern wonder. Tie this together with one of the more intriguing cyberpunk franchises out there and you have a great recipe for an instant classic of a video game.

Don't go in expecting a Deus Ex or Cyberpunk 2077; this game is linear almost to a fault. There is virtually zero exploration and the storylines don't really branch beyond some basic choice-and-consequence. The greatest shame to this linearity is the fact that the Shadowrun franchise is extremely compelling. It marries traditional fantasy with the dystopian themes of the cyberpunk genre, creating a world that has literal technomancy: magic and technology together. This is a fresh concept, indeed, as most cyberpunk content focuses more on the classic definition of "high tech, low life". Shadowrun takes that and blends it with mystic elements to create something that truly stands out among the genre. As a result, I just want to take my time and really explore the world and concept that Jordan Weisman devised.. but due to this game's linearity, the full extent of this exploration is limited to simply looking at the game world as I progress through it. Fortunately, this game's art is phenomenal.

That leads me to point out two of the game's strongest points: storytelling and atmosphere. Due to the linearity of the game, the story is very focused. It's not about accumulating side quests and grinding to max levels. This game is about creating a character you want to play and then progressing through a great story, meeting memorable characters and just soaking in the exceptional cyberpunk atmosphere. Despite being an isometric RPG, this game has absolutely zero trouble immersing me fully into the world. The game's story does a solid job of not only immersing the player into the world but it also really serves to teach new players the core principles and lore of the series. That's something that not every game can pull off easily. The atmosphere constantly gives the player the feeling of living in a near-future world where technology and society have gone wrong; with magic added to the mix, it truly gives the game an ambient sense of oppression, like society is truly teetering on the edge of total collapse.

I should also mention that the game's combat system is actually quite solid. I'm NOT a fan of turn-based combat systems at all (with the exception of Larian's Divinity: Original Sin games). That being said, Shadowrun Returns' combat system is simplistic in a great way and manages to somehow avoid many of the things that typically frustrate me about this sort of combat. I've seen many compare the game's combat to XCOM and while I own an XCOM game, I have yet to play it so I can't really speak as to the accuracy of that comparison. All I CAN say, however, is that it gives me classic Fallout vibes, minus some of the really irritating aspects of those games' combat systems. It's a simple as action points that determine how far you can maneuver and whether or not you can even fire your weapon. It's certainly nowhere near Larian's level of brilliance but it serves its purpose well. I've never once felt irritated/frustrated by this game's combat which is a MAJOR accomplishment for a turn-based combat system, in my book.

Overall, as long as you go in with realistic expectations and as long as you have at least a passing interest in the cyberpunk genre, I'm certain you'll enjoy this game. I actually bought this game well over a year ago in response to my first bit of interest that I had toward the then-upcoming Cyberpunk 2077 and it served as a pretty decent introduction to the genre. I followed it up by buying the rest of the trilogy and the entire Deus Ex series and now, with 2077 finally out, I consider myself to be quite a passionate fan of this genre of fiction... but I digress, this game is fantastic and I definitely recommend it. Just remember that this isn't Fallout, Baldur's Gate, etc. It's very linear, but it's extremely well-written and soaked with cyberpunk atmosphere. If you're looking for a fun game to play on the side while enjoying Cyberpunk 2077, or just want to give this genre a shot, definitely consider grabbing this one!

Shadowrun Returns is an top-down isometric RPG game, set in the universe of the Shadowrun pen & paper role-playing game.

You take direct control of your central character, followed by the companions you choose or forced to by the game. Combat mode is activated when you encounter aggressive NPCs. Combat options include using cover, summoning creatures to fight for you, healing and boosting your team, spells, melee weapons and gun play. You have direct control of your own team. Interaction with the world and team is highly limited when out of combat unfortunately. 

When you start a game, you pick your character's gender, race (human, elf, ork, dwarf or troll) and either pick a pre-designed class or build your own. The character creation and progression system is highly flexible, you are given points which you allocate to certain abilities, enhancing them or giving you more options. You earn more of these by progressing through the plot or doing side quests in game. Throughout the game, you can also learn new spells, buy new weapons or invest in implants (at the expense of your ability to cast spells).

The default campaign that comes with the game is short, linear, and filled with plenty of good and interesting characters that aren't fully fleshed out. Good plot, but missed opportunity. User generated campaigns are hit and miss, but some surpassing the default campaign.

Graphics look beautiful, and really delivers the cyberpunk look and feel. Music and sound effects are good, but with only a limited selection, you end up hearing the same few tracks and sounds often. 

TL:DR: good for scratching that old-school isometric RPG itch, some good strategic choices to make in the game. The default campaign is fine, but limited, might want to check out the user made stuff, or DLC.

[b]+++ Shadowrun: What Is It? +++[/b]
I recommend this game highly for those who have never touched anything Shadowrun before, as it provides a very good first step into the world of Shadowrun. Shadowrun began as a pen-and-paper RPG in the 80's created by the at the time popular tabletop games company FASA. FASA and Jordan Weisman created the Shadowrun universe, along with it's more popular big brother Battletech, and it's much less popular (but still beloved) little sister Crimson Skies. Shadowrun started small, but over time with the release of sourcebooks it became an extremely richly developed world with a lore content amount easily able to rival that of the likes of D&D and Warhammer: 40k. It received it's first and only major video game title in 1993 & 1994, for the SNES and Sega Genesis respectively. When FASA died, Shadowrun passed through many different hands and received new iterations, but really was never heard from in the video gaming industry again... until Harebrained Schemes (owned by Jordan Weisman, Shadowrun's creator and father) crowdfunded Shadowrun Returns.

Shadowrun itself is a world of exotic magic and technological wonders, a world of interest and intrigue. It combines classic D&D fantasy tropes into a near-future cyberpunk sci-fi landscape all whilst adding and seasoning the pot with a pinch of it's own uniqueness in order to create one of the most beloved franchises ever. Shadowrun takes place in the "Sixth World" which came about after the Mayan Calendar ended in 2012 ushering in a new cycle and heralding the return of magic to the world. People started to transform into and give birth to metahumans (elves, dwarves, orcs, and trolls), people were capable of real magic, and mythological creatures such as minotaurs, centaurs, and even dragons started appearing the world over. The return of magic wasn't the only major change in the world however, as "too-big-to-fail" corporations were growing ever larger, becoming megacorporations and amassing power almost equal to that of actual nations, such to the point that many of the countries of the world granted them extra-territoriality, basically giving them the rights to act as their own country on any property they owned. Technology has made huge leaps, even going as far as to create a virtual matrix which is essentially the entire internet given life through VR. Shadowrun is very much both fantasy and sci-fi, though it brings it's own version of grimdark to the table in the realization that the world is now more-or-less ruled by megacorps, and everyone from the leaders of nations and CEO's of megacorps down to lowly priests and Lone Star detectives are all playing the "great game", everyone has an agenda, everyone has a move to make, and everyone is out for themselves. No one is to be trusted, there's no sense of unity, and individual's are valued by the size of their wallet.

Where you come in is within the shadowy world of Shadowrunning. In regards to both international laws as well as corporate laws, shadowrunning is highly illegal. That doesn't stop it from happening however, for in the world of Shadowrun - if it exists then there's a market for it. Are you a corp. CEO who wants to steal valuable research data from another larger rival corporation without having it traced back to you? Hire a runner. Are you a government agent investigating the shady doings of a company, though due to the laws of extra-territoriality you can't carry out your investigation properly because the areas that hold the company's darkest secrets are restricted access by law? Hire a runner. Are you an underworld crime lord who needs a package of uncertain legitimacy to be delivered through a highly secured area? Hire a runner. If there's a job that needs doing that you can't be connected to, there is always someone willing to get their hands dirty for you... provided you can have the nuyen.

[b]+++ The Game Review +++[/b]

[b]Character Creation[/b]
Shadowrun Returns does a decent job at letting you create the character you want to be. Want to be a Troll who is an incredibly talented Shaman that also dabbles in Decking (hacking) on the side? Sure. Want to be an Elven gunslinger who can throw a fireball just as fast as he can draw a gun from a holster? Go ahead. Maybe you're just the average human that doesn't know squat about magic or hacking, but can fire a shotgun or an assault rifle just as well as the next guy. Whatever tickles your fancy, Shadowrun can accommodate you. For the most part. That is to say that just like any other game, you can expect limitations regarding what's possible. For example, the game isn't going to let you be a dragon, nor is it going to let you be an immortal Elf from the 4th World with immense magical power.

[b]The Gameplay[/b]
The Gameplay of Shadowrun Returns is a mixture between RPG and tactical party-shooter. The action of Shadowrun Returns, of which there is a lot of it, plays like a light X Com-lite. It is essentially this: you get a party of one to four characters which fight in a isometric turn based combat system. Cover is simplified and while flanking can have an effect tactically it doesn't give any bonuses. In terms of tactical combat it's very basic, but the good part is that there is a lot of variety in ways you can win. The gameplay is a bit lacking, but it's good enough to be passable.

[b]Role-playing Elements & Atmosphere:[/b]
The role playing elements honestly lacks a bit. First, there are no major decisions you can make to effect the world around you, it's very linear in that you're expected to follow the story. There is variety in the conversation options but they really don't effect gameplay choices, sadly. In a sense - the roleplaying aspect is more of a personal thing. The ability to roleplay is there, but it doesn't effect gameplay and is really only there for flavoring. The progress of the game itself is pretty linear. Combat is also king unfortunately, so you can't build a character that specializes in talking his way out of situations. Similarly, decking is used primarily for combat and you won't be able to use the skill to bypass major obstacles.

The atmosphere on the other hand is amazing. The game does a near-perfect job to make you really [i]feel[/i] like you're in the world of Shadowrun. The grimdark feel is captured nicely, and all of the areas and characters have a uniqueness to them. No two different areas within this game should ever feel the same to you, and the main cast is colorful and unique, though the minor characters are a bit bland at times. That all said, the atmosphere does well to immerse you in the world.

[b]Graphics/Sound:[/b]
Graphics have never been a majorly important thing to me, however with that said the graphics on this game should be considered very decent, if not at the least acceptable to those who do care about graphics. The gameplay sounds are very much that of stock sounds, passable but nothing incredible. The soundtrack on the other hand is purely Amazing with a capital A. Even for people who never heard of the composer, the soundtrack does an absolutely amazing job in further immersing you in the grimdark near-future Seattle.

[b]+++ Final Thoughts +++[/b]
Shadowrun is a great game and a great first step into the universe, though it isn't without it's problems. The combat is a bit light on the tactical side, though it does have lots of variety which makes up for that in spades. For me where the game loses points is in it's cardboard RP aspects. Your decisions effect nothing, every problem is solved with a gun, and the story is linear. That said, the atmosphere is greatly immersive and all-in-all the game results in one hell of an experience. Despite it setbacks this game provides a great core experience, even disregarding Shadowrun's charisma.

[b]Score:[/b]
If you love the Shadowrun universe: 8/10
If you don't care about Shadowrun and just want a solid game: 7/10
Is it recommended?: Absolutely yes!

So I played the Shadowrun games slightly out of order yet that did not hamper my enjoyment of Shadowrun Returns.  For those unfamiliar with this series Shadowrun started out as a tabletop RPG and has seamlessly made the transition into a computer RPG series thanks to the team at Harebrained Schemes.  These are very much story-driven games featuring a brilliant tactical combat system to support the gameplay.  I loved Shadowrun Dragonfall when I played through it close to five years ago and I finally got the chance to play the Returns, the first game in the series.  As someone who likes to play lots of different games it is always a challenge to commit myself to a lengthy RPG.  That said I find the Shadowrun universe such a interesting setting and I'm so glad I had the chance to revisit it.

Shadowrun Returns starts when you get a video message on your computer from someone you used go running with.  See shadow runners are freelancers who get paid to do other peoples dirty work.  Turns out your friend Sam has met his end and he is offering you a reward if you can find out who killed him.  If working for a dead man isn't interesting enough you start to unravel much bigger plots at play.  You'll start by investigating the local bar where Sam used to spend much of his time at.  Conveniently this bar happens to be a great place to pick up some jobs and the supplies need to go along with them.  Eventually you meet one of Sam's relatives and find out they have ties to the Universal Brotherhood, a religious organization which, after some investigating, appears to have some nasty secrets going on behind the scenes.


You'll spend an equal amount of time or more in battle as you will reading the massive script that makes up the storyline.  Shadowrun Returns is a tactical strategy game where you'll find your team and the opposing forces on a large grid often compose of multiple rooms and scattered furniture.  You and your opponents takes turns and on your turn each of your characters usually have two actions they can take.  Whether you move, attack, or use an ability these each will take one action point.  When you go to attack an enemy you see a percentage of the chance that you'll land a hit on them.  This percentage has many factors that go into it such as the distance between you and your foe, your proficiency level with your weapon, and whether your opponent is out in the open or behind cover.

Only your main character will you need to level up stats for as all your other companions you'll just hire from the local network of available shadow runners.  There are some major skills such as Quickness, Strength, Intelligence, and Willpower.  Each of these skills has subcategories which can only be leveled up to as far as you have leveled the overlapping skill.  This means it will probably be best to focus on two or three areas to specialize in rather than attempt to be a jack of all trades.  There are different archetypes that specialize in close quarters combat, magic abilities, decking (hacking), summoning spirits, and rigging drones.  Having a team that compliments your own skills and gives you flexibility in combat is key to surviving the rather unforgiving scenarios throughout the game.

I've always enjoy tactical RPGs from Final Fantasy Tactics Advance to Banner Saga and I can confidently say that the Shadowrun series can easily stand with the greats.  What is most unique about Shadowrun is the incredible universe the games are set in which combines cyberpunk and fantasy in a wholly-believable modern setting.  Even aside from the deep and fascinating storytelling is a equally complex but manageable combat system and character progression.  As you barely get through one fight to another each new upgrade you receive feels like a godsend and will provide just the edge you need to survive your next encounter.  There is a lot of reading to get through to enjoy the storyline but if you don't mind that and wish to sink your teeth into a deeply rewarding tactical RPG look no farther than Shadowrun Returns.

I don't have time anymore for 150 hours of generic fantasy tropes. A huge disappointment.  I was really looking forward to this game since it showed up on Kickstarter.  Fallout 1 & 2 are among my favorite games ever, and this was touted as a return to that style of RPG.  It...isn't.

I find the combat enjoyable.  It's basically a simplified version of XCOM:  Enemy Unknown.  One problem with it is that once combat starts, it doesn't end until you move to another map, even if there are no enemies around.  So after a fight ends, you'll have to move your party through the map in turn-based mode until you get to an exit.

The story is good by video game standards.  You receive a recorded message from an old friend who's been murdered and are tasked with tracking down his killer.  For the most part, dialogue is well-written.  There's no voice acting, which some may take issue with, but it allows for more robust dialogue.  Unfortunately, this game doesn't take advantage of that benefit.

The game is extraordinarily linear.  There's exactly one path through the story.  A handful of situations where you may be able to get from point A to point B by a slightly different route exist (i.e., bluff your way past a guard vs. hacking through an unguarded door), but these are so few and so insignificant that they don't make any real difference overall.  Dialogue is pretty much the same no matter what:  Ask about story-related stuff, ask about general backround/setting information.  Very little opportunity to employ your character's personality.

Sidequests are almost nonexistent, and the few that the game does have are simple "go over there and get me that thing," or "while you're on this run, see if you can find a thing I want" sorts of things.

The whole game is designed entirely around mobile devices and it suffers for it.  The UI is a bit clunky and unintuitive for PC, limited to what would work on a touch-based interface.  The save system is simply unacceptable.  The game has no manual save option.  Not even a save and quit function.  It's entirely based on reaching checkpoints.  This is supposed to be fixed with the DLC scheduled for January 2014, but until then, if you screw up a fight at the end of a mission?  You're replaying the whole mission.  Have to leave before you finish a mission?  You're replaying the whole mission.  As I understand it, this is because the game cannot save the current map state, which explains some of the linearity.  When you return to a location, you're actually loading a completely different map of the location with its own triggers, different versions of NPCs with dialogue appropriate to that point in the story, etc.  This means that the player can't affect any change in the game as every change or combination of changes to a location would require its own unique map, and I'm not even sure if the game is able to load different versions of the same map based on variables.

I can't really speak to the user-generated content as I haven't used the editor or played any user-made campaigns yet, but from what I've heard from those who have, the editor is very, very limited in what it can do.  As a result, a lot of people who were planning on making content for the game have given up.

Maybe the upcoming DLC will improve the editor, maybe (probably) it won't.  Either way, I wouldn't suggest paying more than about $5 for Shadowrun Returns.

relatively short fun isometric  strategy/rpg title. 
the story moves through the missions. in this regard this game is closer to any strategy game campaign, like, say, starcraft, where you are locked inside each mission and can't go back or decide the order of doing things in your walkthrough, rather then rpg titles like baldur's gate, where you have an open world to explore. 
shadowrun has very little side quests, so you are basically going through main quest from start to finish, occasionally taking side jobs, when they are available.
the plot itself is absurd but somewhat charming and, most importantly, it opens an  opportunity for implementing unique game mechanics, and we all gathered here for the gameplay, right?
shadowrun has a mix of genres thrown together and tossed hard: it is a fantasy, but also a cyberpunk universe, it has magic, and technology, and shamanism, and shi-fi elements, and everything is written like a noir mystery novel. if you are looking for a literature masterpiece, you probably will be disappointed, but if you don't mind a bit of corny and wacky for sake of entertainment, give it a try.
now for the good stuff: gameplay. you have your turn-based fights, 3 actions per turn, a decent range of weapons, several type of magic including summoning spirits, and hacking. if the mission has a hacking part it is the most fun. you need to make sure your hacker arrived safely to the spot where he can connect to the matrix and defend him, while he acts inside the matrix. so you have a 2-dimensional stage of events, where you switch between the matrix and the real world - never played anything like that.
the rpg parts are pretty unique too. you earn karma points for the missions and spend those for your stats and skills. the further you go to the certain tree, the more expensive is the next step, however you have a lot of room for the experimentation, you have enough karma to make anything from any class you started with,  from a decent jack of all trades to a glasscanon (me every time lol). 
despite being an old and somewhat unforgiving game (no, you can't re-speck) the in-game instructions on classes ans karma are very good. you can build a character and complete the game just using provided info, no need of reading 1000s of pages of guides on making a character (looking at you, underrail)
the game itself has only 1 campaign, but if you want more, there is plenty additional missions at steam workshop.
overall, nice game, can be enjoyable, can be frustrating, can be beaten in a couple of evenings
